{"approach":"From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail through the beaver meadows; at the first switchback past the meadows, beyond the Colchuck/Stuart Lake trail fork, leave the trail to the south on an obscure, unmaintained climbers' path, crossing Stuart Lake creek on logs, to reach the base of the northeast-facing couloir below Sherpa Peak. The path is unmaintained and can be hard to follow.","itinerary":"Approach from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to a camp in the basin between Sherpa and Argonaut below the couloir; alpine-start to climb the couloir (snow/ice to roughly 50 degrees) to its top, then scramble up and right to the Balanced Rock summit via a short 5.0 pitch; descend the same route or via Sherpa Pass."}

{"approach":"Start at the Longs Pass Trailhead (Esmeralda TH) at the end of Teanaway River Road (USFS Rd 9737) out of the North Fork Teanaway. Take Longs Pass Trail #1229 climbing steadily through open pine forest and sagebrush switchbacks for about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft of gain (roughly 1.5-2 hours) to Longs Pass at approximately 6,200-6,400 ft, which opens up the first views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, and the Stuart Range crest. From the pass, drop off the north side on a steep, loose, eroded boot path (sometimes called the 'tapeworm') losing about 1,400-1,600 ft over roughly a mile to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft; this descent tread is dirt/scree and can be slick and hard on the knees. Ford Ingalls Creek (a rock-hop in low water, but a genuine wet crossing during early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it east/downstream about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at roughly 4,700 ft - the last dependable water source before the alpine basin above. From the junction, a climbers' boot path (referenced in trip reports as 'Variation #1' toward Mount Stuart) switchbacks up through forest and talus; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide separating two gullies, then drop into the eastern gully, which leads more directly toward Sherpa Peak. Class 2 slopes above the gully lead to 'Table Rock,' a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the boulder-choked Sherpa-Argonaut basin, a common high bivy for parties splitting the approach over two days. From Table Rock, a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the Stuart Range divide, putting climbers on the ridge crest east of the balanced rock; follow the crest west over blocks and sandy, exposed benches (Class 3-4) to reach the base of the balanced rock formation itself, where the Standard Route begins with a shoulder-stand or rope-lasso move to gain the east-side pedestal, then bolt-protected friction climbing (5.7) to the summit block. Car-to-base is roughly 6-7 miles one-way with roughly 6,000 ft of climbing on the way in, and Longs Pass to regain on the way out; expect loose rock and real route-finding through the gully/basin section, and carry all the water you'll need above the Beverly-Turnpike junction since the upper basin is dry.","approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"The base is a free-standing pillar, not a face, and that is why this one cannot be mistaken once you are close. From Table Rock a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the range divide, putting you on the crest east of the balanced rock. Follow the crest west over blocks and sandy exposed benches at Class 3-4 until you are standing at the foot of a detached granite pillar. That pillar is the route.

The move at the base is the proof: you cannot simply start climbing. Gaining the pedestal at the bottom needs a shoulder-stand off a partner, or a rope thrown or lassoed over the point of the pedestal. If you have found a start you can climb unaided, you are on the peak's ordinary ridge scrambling and not on this feature.

Second confirmation, and it is unusual for the range: above the pedestal the climbing is bolt-protected friction at about 5.7 to a flat top, with a single ageing bolt up there used to rappel back down. Bolts on Sherpa are rare enough that finding them is strong positive evidence.

Direction check in cloud: you arrive at the crest east of the pillar and walk west to it. If you are heading east along the crest you are walking away from the rock and from Sherpa's true summit, which lies beyond the rock to the west.

And a scope warning worth reading before you commit: this is not a route up the mountain. It is the technical feature near the summit, and most parties combine it with the Class 3-4 ridge traverse to Sherpa's main summit. If your objective was the peak, the pillar is an add-on rather than the way up.","distMi":6.5,"hazards":["A steep, loose descent off Longs Pass in both directions","An Ingalls Creek ford that is a genuine crossing in early-season snowmelt","Loose rockfall-prone gully and basin terrain — helmets strongly advised","A dry upper basin: no water above the Beverly-Turnpike junction","An exposed Class 3-4 crest traverse to reach the pillar","A single ageing bolt as the rappel anchor off the top","The unroped downclimb back to camp can take as long as the technical pitch itself"],"name":"Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and Table Rock","notes":"From the Esmeralda / Longs Pass trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take Longs Pass Trail #1229 through open pine and sage switchbacks about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft.

Drop off the north side on the steep eroded boot path, losing 1,400-1,600 ft over about a mile to Ingalls Creek at roughly 4,800 ft. Ford the creek — a rock-hop in low water, a real wet crossing in snowmelt — and follow the Ingalls Creek Trail east about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike junction at about 4,700 ft. That junction is the last dependable water before the alpine basin.

Do not confuse the table rock (7,400 ft, a bivy shelf) with the balanced rock (on the summit ridge, a perched block); they are different features doing different jobs.

orig: {"approach":"The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 28 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. {"approach":"From the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead (Bean Creek/Beverly Creek TH) off the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR-9737-112), the approach is well-documented with concrete checkpoints: at about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike Trail) — a wrong fork onto the Bean Creek Trail here is a commonly reported mistake, so double-check the sign. At about 3.1 miles, turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek Trail). At about 3.6 miles you crest Fourth Creek Pass with the first open views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. Continue down the far side to about 6 miles and ~4,200 ft, where you ford Ingalls Creek (wading or a footlog) to reach good flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence — day one is roughly 6 miles and 2,000 ft of gain. From camp, follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west for about half a mile, then cut sharply left (north) and start climbing straight upslope toward Argonaut's south face: expect brushy 'jackstraw' forest for the first 300 vertical feet and then dense slide alder for close to 1,000 feet above that (progress can slow to a few hundred feet per hour in the thick of it — stay right/climber's-right to minimize brush where possible). At about 5,200 ft the brush relents onto open slopes; ascend the left side of a large drainage gully up to about 6,600 ft, then continue up the gully itself. At about 7,100 ft the gully forks — the standard line is the left branch (the right also goes but is less traveled). At the base of the summit face, start in the rightmost and larger of two short left-facing corners and climb about three pitches of blocky rock to the summit. The 50-foot chockstone gully that tops out on the east ridge (Class 4, stepping right at the overhang) is the finish of the scramble route, not part of this climb; it is the usual way down. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford, sustained brush-bashing on the lower slopes, and possible snow in the gully in shoulder season (carry an axe/crampons if conditions warrant).","approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"Two tests, one at the gully fork and one at the wall, and you need both.

First, the fork at about 7,100 ft. The gully you have been climbing splits. The standard line is the left branch. The right branch also reaches the mountain but is far less travelled, so a party that drifts right will find progressively less sign of passage — that absence is the signal to come back down and cross over.

Second, the wall itself, and this is the one that matters in fog because the gully fork can be ambiguous under snow. At the base of the south face there are two short left-facing corners side by side. The route starts in the rightmost and larger of the two. Not a corner — two corners, and you take the bigger, right-hand one. If there is only one corner in front of you, you are not at the start.

What the climbing should feel like, as a check on all of the above: blocky, generally solid rock, three pitches, graded 5.6 — but an old-school 5.6 that parties consistently report climbing like modern 5.9 or harder. So sustained-feeling climbing is not evidence you are off route here. Watch for a few loose blocks low down.

A separate feature worth not confusing with the start: high on the mountain there is a 50-foot gully with a chockstone near its top, Class 4, taken by stepping right at the overhang, which tops out on the east ridge a short way from the summit. That is the finish of the ordinary scramble line, and the approach description on this route describes it as though it were the route. Descend the far side to roughly 6 miles and 4,200 ft, ford Ingalls Creek, and camp at the Fourth Creek confluence. Day one is about 6 miles and 2,000 ft.

From camp, follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west about half a mile, then cut sharply left and north and climb straight upslope. Expect roughly 300 vertical feet of tangled forest and then close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above that — progress can drop to a few hundred feet an hour.

At about 5,200 ft the brush relents. Climb the left side of a large drainage gully to about 6,600 ft, then the gully itself.","season":"Roughly Jul-Sep. {"approach":"Northeast via Longs Pass Trail #1229 and Ingalls Way Trail #1390; ascend first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir","approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"The cirque is the arrival, and it is unmistakable even in cloud because it closes around you. You climb loose ground for a long time and then the walls come up on three sides — very steep cliffs at about 8,700 ft with the summit directly above. That enclosure is the cue. Scree that keeps going with open ground on both sides means you are still below it.

Which clearing, which is the actual problem: from the Ingalls Creek trail, count west from where the Longs Pass trail came down to the creek. The correct line is the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. Ulrich's is the big obvious gully; if you are ascending a defined gully rather than an open clearing, you are in Ulrich's itself and on a different route entirely. And if the clearing you picked is east of that point, you are heading for the Cascadian Couloir — the standard walk-up and the usual descent — which is easier ground and will not put you under a headwall.

Confirmation at the base: the technical pitches start up the centre of the headwall, and they top out very close to the true summit. Nothing on this route is harder than 5.7. If the ground in front of you looks harder than that, you have drifted to one side of the centre.

Preview it from Longs Pass. This is the rare approach where the whole objective is visible from a trail junction two thirds of the way through the day, and a party that identifies the headwall and the correct clearing from the pass essentially cannot get this wrong afterwards.","distMi":2.5,"hazards":["Frequent rockfall in the cirque and on the headwall, made worse by other parties","Sustained loose scree and choss on the ascent to the cirque, with no trail","A steep eroded descent path off Longs Pass, hard on the knees in both directions","An Ingalls Creek crossing that is a genuine ford in early-season snowmelt","Early-season snow and ice in the cirque","Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above the clearing"],"name":"Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir","notes":"From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Longs Pass trail up open pine and sage switchbacks to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200 ft. Stop here — this is the one place on the whole day where you can see the entire south side of the mountain at once, and five minutes spent picking out the headwall from the pass is worth an hour of guessing later.

Drop off the north side of the pass on the steep, eroded boot path to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and join the Ingalls Creek trail.

Then the key move: from where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, go west along the creek trail and take the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. That clearing is the line of ascent.

Above the clearing it is sustained scree and choss up to a cirque at about 8,700 ft. The technical climbing — five pitches, never harder than 5.7, plus a lot of fourth and easy fifth — starts up the centre of the headwall from there.","season":"Roughly Jun-Aug, with July the usual month; late season the loose ground below the headwall gets worse rather than better"}]}

orig: {"approach":"The genuine standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of South Peak's granite faces; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.","approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"Do not start under the summit — walk south along the foot of the ridge past it. The start is a pair of clean dihedrals side by side on the ridge's west flank, and the pair is the test: two obvious corners, either of which will take you to the crest, with nothing else of the kind nearby. Both give about a rope length of climbing on chickenheads and good face features once you step right out of the corner. The second confirmation is overhead and unmistakable: look along the ridge crest above you for the Cannonhole, a gap punched clean through the ridge, which the route traverses on its second pitch. If you cannot see a hole through the crest from where you are standing, you are not below this line. Negative markers: if you are under a single chimney tucked into the left side of a face directly beneath the summit, you have stopped short and are at the west face route; if you are on glacier ice with a moat between you and the rock, you have gone round to the east side entirely.","hazards":["Long, committing off-trail approach with glacier travel","The cannonhole gap on the traverse pitch is exposed and the feature is relatively young rock","Weather-window dependent — this is a remote crest with no quick way off","Both start dihedrals look alike; picking the wrong one is harmless, picking the wrong face is not"],"name":"Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor","notes":"From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor over Itswoot Ridge and Cub Lake and up Bachelor Creek. Off-trail, brushy, and with glacier travel before you reach the peaks; a full day or two of approach is normal. orig: {"waypoints":[{"directions":"From Bellingham, take Interstate 5 to the Sunset Drive/Mount Baker exit and follow the Mount Baker Highway (WA-542) east through Glacier, the last place to resupply groceries, to the Nooksack River bridge about 13 miles past town. The road washes out at 2.3 miles; park there at Ruth Creek, about 2,156 feet, since the road is not drivable beyond that point. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit is required for overnight stays: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee, reserved on Recreation.gov. orig: {"waypoints":[{"directions":"Drive SR 706 east through Ashford to the Nisqually Entrance of Mount Rainier National Park, then 6.5 miles on to Longmire. The road is paved and open essentially year round, conditions permitting. Park at Longmire and register at the Wilderness Information Center before you start.","distMi":0,"elev":2749,"lat":46.7502,"lng":-121.8124,"name":"Longmire Wilderness Information Center (Wonderland Trail)","note":"Register the climb and pick up the wilderness permit here before starting up the Wonderland Trail.","type":"Trailhead"},{"directions":"Follow the Wonderland Trail from Longmire. About 3 miles out it drops steeply to the log crossing of Kautz Creek, which debris flows periodically wreck, so ask about it at the Wilderness Information Center. Beyond the creek the trail switchbacks through old growth, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek and passes Devil's Dream camp before opening into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at the 1915 patrol cabin.","distMi":7,"elev":5300,"lat":46.79417,"lng":-121.83889,"name":"Indian Henry's Hunting Ground (patrol cabin)","note":"Historic 1915 patrol cabin marks where the route leaves the maintained Wonderland Trail for cross-country travel toward the Mirror Lakes basin.","type":"Junction"},{"directions":"Leave the maintained Wonderland Trail at the patrol cabin and take the Mirror Lakes spur west, crossing marshy meadow on a series of plank walkways. Maintained tread ends part way along and the path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft, in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak, roughly a mile off the Wonderland. These tarns are the last dependable water before the dry south-west and west slopes of Pyramid Peak.","distMi":8,"elev":5600,"lat":46.7957,"lng":-121.8415,"name":"Mirror Lakes","note":"Small tarns about a mile off the Wonderland Trail; last dependable water before contouring dry southwest/west slopes of Pyramid Peak.","type":"Water"},{"directions":"From the tarns it is cross-country travel. Head north-east out of the basin and contour the south-west then west slopes of Pyramid Peak, staying roughly between 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. There is no boot-pack and only sparse cairning through here, so carry a map or GPS track and expect to find your own line; snowmelt water is often available around the point into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak near 6,300 ft is a common first night.","distMi":9.5,"elev":6631,"lat":46.8106,"lng":-121.8127,"name":"Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)","note":"Flat campsites just north of this 6,631 ft high point give broad views of Success Cleaver.","type":"Campsite"},{"directions":"Drop north-north-east from Point 6631 a short way to the saddle at about 6,400 ft, which is the start of Success Cleaver proper. It is a scree and loose-boulder col and it looks unpleasant, which is how you know it is the right place. There is an easier way down into it than the obvious line, and parties record missing it and taking the worst ground, so pick the descent out before you commit and note it for the return.","distMi":10,"elev":6400,"lat":null,"lng":null,"name":"6,400 ft saddle below Success Cleaver","note":"Short descent NNE from Point 6631 to this saddle; typical high camp before scrambling onto the lower cleaver at first light.","type":"Campsite"},{"directions":"From the col the cleaver rises straight ahead and does not let up: loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, no track and no cairned line, weaving among rock towers on ground you route-find yourself. Use what is on either side as the test. The South Tahoma Glacier should fall away to climber's left and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to climber's right; if you find yourself on a glacier, or if the going out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you have drifted off the cleaver and are contouring around Pyramid Peak instead. Rockfall risk rises sharply with any party above you, the rock firms up above roughly 7,000 ft, and there are bivy sites around 8,100 to 8,300 ft.","distMi":11,"elev":8200,"lat":null,"lng":null,"name":"Lower Success Cleaver gendarmes","note":"Loose rock towers force weaving route-finding on the lower rib; rockfall risk climbs if other parties are above; bivy options around 8,100-8,300 ft.","type":"Hazard"},{"directions":"Follow the cleaver crest up through class 3 and short class 4 rock bands and steep chutes, past bivy benches near 9,400 ft and the small col at about 10,700 ft. Higher, the crest holds a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow has melted off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies and across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall, joining the Kautz Cleaver between roughly 12,200 and 12,600 ft. Cross those chutes early, before the sun starts releasing rock and ice; helmets on.","distMi":12.3,"elev":12600,"lat":46.843829,"lng":-121.768939,"name":"Rockfall chutes to Kautz Cleaver headwall","note":"Angle across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall and gain the Kautz Cleaver near 12,600 ft; helmet mandatory, best crossed before sun loosens rock.","type":"Hazard"},{"directions":"From the Kautz Cleaver climb steepening snow and ice, generally around 45 degrees, to the headwall below the summit. A cliff band bars the way and is passed either by a short low fifth class rock step, exposed and sometimes wet or icy, or by an isolated snow and ice pitch of about 15 ft at up to 55 degrees, depending on the season. Above it the angle eases onto the summit plateau at Point Success, 14,158 ft.","elev":14158,"elevFt":14158,"lat":46.8459412,"lng":-121.7675967,"name":"Point Success","type":"Summit"}]}

orig: {"approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"From the tarns of Upper Royal Basin, look up at the Needles wall and pick out the northeast-facing gully on the climber's-right side of the group. Early in the season it holds snow, which makes it the obvious white line on an otherwise dry face and is the easiest identification you will get. Cross the talus to its foot; the base is where the loose scree fan narrows and steepens into the gully proper. Climb it and watch for the dogleg — the gully bends left below a notch on the summit ridge, and that bend is the confirmation you are in the right one rather than a neighbour. From the notch a short, exposed Class 3 scramble runs south to the true summit. The Needles hold several similar gullies and Clark stands immediately northwest with Johnson west, so a peak that looks right from the basin may not be the one you want. Higher up, on the broken ledges, one spot appears to cliff out where a cairned Class 3 crack around the corner is the way through. Arrival: a saddle is the low point between two rises. From it, this route climbs the southwest face, and the descent runs back down near the northwest ridge toward the same saddle. If the ground above you steepens into a face rather than a ridge, that is the route. Why there is so little here, said plainly: Swiss Peak has one described route and no first-ascent record, the peak itself is not precisely located, and nothing published locates a feature at the foot of the southwest face. What is locatable is the saddle and the ridge. Do not expect a cairn, a gully or a flake to confirm you; expect the shape of the col. Day 2 — climb Access Creek drainage to the Luna Cirque basin, gain Luna Col, camp near Luna Col or continue toward East/West Fury. Day 3 — traverse East Fury, West Fury, cross the glacier/snowfield to the Swiss-Fury saddle, climb Swiss Peak's southwest face, continue toward Spectre Plateau. Day 4-5 — continue over Phantom Peak, Crooked Thumb, to Mt. Challenger and Whatcom Pass, exiting via Chilliwack River or Little Beaver trails. Baker Highway/SR 542, GPS approx. 48.847, -121.693) walk to the northwest corner of the large paved parking lot — the signed Table Mountain Trail #681 starts opposite the vault toilets, on the side of the lot away from the highway. The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path that climbs gently before reaching its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there the route ascends a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — this is the crux of the approach: a narrow, exposed catwalk with steep drop-offs toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek drainage 400-800 ft below. Footing here is loose rock and gravel over hard-packed tread, and snow or verglas frequently lingers in this cliff section into July, making it the most hazardous stretch of the whole route; many parties turn back here in early season without traction devices. After roughly 400 ft of gain (about 0.4-0.5 mi from the car) the switchbacks top out on the broad, relatively flat summit plateau ("the table"). From here follow the well-trodden tread west/northwest along the south rim, which gives open views straight down onto the Chain Lakes Trail; numerous braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.2 mi you reach the east side of the tabletop with views of Mount Baker and Ptarmigan Ridge, and by 1.3 mi you arrive at two small tarns that frame Mount Shuksan — a natural high point/turnaround for most day hikers and the last easily identified landmark before the trail degrades into a sketchy, unmaintained scramble path descending toward the Table Mountain Glacier. There is no reliable water along the route: the summit tarns are shallow, silty, and not worth treating, so carry all water from the car. Arrival on the table: after roughly 400 ft of gain the switchbacks top out on a broad, relatively flat plateau. Flat ground is the confirmation you are through the cliff band.

From camp, cross toward the deep gully dividing the mountain's south wall from the small semi-detached tower at its lower right, and get onto the tower's own rock on the right side of that gully. Then walk the base of the tower's south face leftward, past the lowest point of the rock, until you are under A pair of parallel cracks. Two cracks side by side, read as one feature. That pair is the landmark; a single crack means you have not reached them.

This route is the right-hand crack of the pair. The test that separates it from its twin is what happens on pitch two. This line's hardest climbing comes higher up and is crack and face — no chimney. The left-hand crack of the pair cruxes in an upper chimney that swallows a large cam.

So: if pitch two puts you inside a chimney wanting big gear, step back down and move one crack right. If pitch two stays out in the open on cracks and face and the hard moves arrive near the top, you are on this route. It also goes a full number grade easier than its twin, so difficulty itself is evidence — a pitch that feels desperate for the grade is a sign you are on the left-hand line.

Negative marker on length and descent. Two pitches. Most parties rappel the route on gear from the top of pitch two and walk down the talus and slabs to the drainage. If you continue and top out on the tower itself, you have committed to a different descent — the north-east gully in three rappels of about seventy-five feet each, a doubled sixty-metre rope for every one, with anchors you may have to build.","hazards":["The route name says west and the rock faces south","Its twin runs parallel a few feet away and is a grade harder with a chimney crux","Committing to the tower's summit changes the descent from a two-rope-length retreat to a gully rappel","Rappel anchors here are not documented as fixed; carry webbing and rings","Remote basin, multi-day walk out, no cell coverage"],"name":"Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the Cathedral-Monk gully","notes":"Paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft, then roughly twelve miles of trail #504 to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and overgrown tread. Down into the next drainage, then a side trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft.

Two to four days for most parties, climbing from camp in the basin. Free self-issue wilderness permit and a parking pass at the trailhead; no cell coverage anywhere on the trip.

As with its twin, this is two pitches at the end of a long walk. It is a companion climb rather than an objective in itself.","season":"Roughly July through the first snow of October"}],"descent_text":"No descent from the top of the second pitch is documented. From camp, cross toward the deep gully dividing the mountain's south wall from the small semi-detached tower at its lower right, and get onto the tower's own rock on the right side of that gully. Then walk the base of the tower's south face leftward, past the lowest point of the rock, until you are under A pair of parallel cracks. Two cracks side by side, read as one feature. That pair is the landmark; a single crack means you have not reached them.

This route is the right-hand crack of the pair. The test that separates it from its twin is what happens on pitch two. This line's hardest climbing comes higher up and is crack and face — no chimney. The left-hand crack of the pair cruxes in an upper chimney that swallows a large cam.

So: if pitch two puts you inside a chimney wanting big gear, step back down and move one crack right. If pitch two stays out in the open on cracks and face and the hard moves arrive near the top, you are on this route. It also goes a full number grade easier than its twin, so difficulty itself is evidence — a pitch that feels desperate for the grade is a sign you are on the left-hand line.

Negative marker on length and descent. Two pitches. Retreating from the top of pitch two means rappelling the route on gear you leave behind, then walking down the talus and slabs to the drainage. orig: {"itinerary":"Day push (the common choice, and no overnight permit is needed): leave the Stuart Lake Trailhead before first light, be at Colchuck Lake around sunrise, at the base of the wall by mid-morning after 3-4 hours of approach, climbing by late morning. The west face is in shade all morning and gets sun in the afternoon, which is a real asset on a cold day and a liability on a hot one. Allow 8 hours or more on the route — the crux pitches reward working the sequences rather than rushing — 1 hour for the descent to the base, and 3 hours to hike out. Realistic car-to-car is 14 to 17 hours; Abegg logged 17 hours 16 minutes for an analogous day on Let it Burn. Two-day version: win or walk up an Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit for the Colchuck zone, hike in on day one to a bivy near the lake or on the boulders in the west basin, climb rested on day two, and hike out that evening. That turns the crux pitches from a stopwatch problem into a climbing problem, and it is the version most parties who send the route describe.","pitch_detail":[{"grade":"5.11","lengthM":20,"notes":"Climb the corner using a variety of techniques; the crux is getting off the ground, with a second hard section mid-pitch. Two-bolt belay.","pitch":"P1"},{"grade":"5.11","lengthM":20,"notes":"Traverse left past bolts with tricky knob wrangling, then layback past more bolts to a two-bolt belay.","pitch":"P2"},{"grade":"5.11+","lengthM":40,"notes":"Climb a seam, make the crux move to gain the crack (the 'flower power crack') on very small gear, then power up the corner to the Sky Lounge — a stellar ledge with two bolts. This is the natural bail point.","pitch":"P3"},{"grade":"5.12","lengthM":45,"notes":"The crux. Traverse right, climb featured slab, punch through an overhanging gold-rock flare, follow the crack to a roof, traverse left, then solve a final boulder problem. Kerwin's Crack (5.12/12+) links into this crux as a harder variation.","pitch":"P4"},{"grade":"5.11-","lengthM":30,"notes":"Hand and finger crack climbing to a sandy alcove belay. End of the route's independent climbing.","pitch":"P5"},{"grade":"5.10a","lengthM":50,"notes":"Joins Let it Burn: a thin corner feature leading to lower-angled slabs and a slab belay. So: Tooth Fairy behind you on the right, big cleaving gully in front of you, start on its left wall.

The hardware test, which works in any visibility: this is an all-bolt line. Quickdraws and nothing else. If you are pulling out cams to protect the first moves, you are on one of the peak's trad routes, not on this one.

The first-pitch grade test: pitch one goes at 5.9 to 5.10a, with an easier 5.8 alternative start bolted to the right. If the first pitch is going at 5.4 you are round on the South Face; if it feels like broken fourth-class scrambling you have not left Pineapple Pass.

And a confirmation higher up for a party that wants one: the third pitch crosses the gully on a large chockstone, and the fourth pitch takes a V-slot at 5.10b. Crossing that gully mid-route on a chockstone is the signature of this line.

Finally, where it puts you: the last bolted anchor is not the summit. One more bolt above it leads onto the North Ridge and about 100 m of unprotected scrambling to the true top. The hardware test, which works in any visibility: this is an all-bolt line. Quickdraws and nothing else. If you are pulling out cams to protect the first moves, you are on one of the peak's trad routes, not on this one.

Coming up the climbers' path into the basin, south Early Winters Spire comes first. You must walk past it. North Early Winters Spire is beyond, and this route is on its west face, reached by traversing left along the base.

So the negative test is: if you have stopped at the first wall you reached, you are under South Early Winters Spire, which carries its own cluster of west-side routes and is a different peak.

The feature that separates the two spires, and it is the best landmark in this basin: a massive chasm, a chockstone-filled chimney, splits North and South Early Winters Spires. It is the Chockstone Route's line. You must have that chasm behind you or beside you before you are under North Early Winters Spire's west face.

Arrival: this route shares its start with the Northwest Corner, reached by traversing left along the base after passing the chasm. It also sits immediately right of Labor Pains, which climbs the clean face between the Chockstone Route and this one. So the order across this wall, from the chasm outward, is: Chockstone Route in the chasm, Labor Pains on the clean face beyond it, then the west face.

Descent, which gives you a third confirmation if you top out unsure: two options exist. The original drops down the left side through a notch with three single-rope rappels, including one free-hanging rappel over a chockstone, and finishes with scrambling back to the base. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the moat between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the south peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.","season":"Jul-Oct"},{"baseFinding":"Once you reach Tupso Pass the route is identical, and the same markers apply: cross to the north side of the ridge past Tin Can Gap to meet the top of the Queest-Alb, find the moat entrance rather than stepping onto open ice, and finish on the three stacked ladders on the south peak.","hazards":["several miles of road walking or biking each way with the resulting late finish","all the hazards of the standard variation once on trail"],"name":"Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41","notes":"FR 41 has washed out repeatedly and the closure point has moved. {"approach":"Drive to Tiffany Springs Campground (elev. ~6,760 ft) via Forest Road 39, accessed either from Conconully (south, via FR-37) or from Winthrop (north, via East Chewuch Road and FR-37) — both are long gravel-road drives of an hour or more. From the campground, hike the Tiffany Lake Trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass (7,150 ft, roughly 45 minutes of easy trail), then leave the trail and traverse south across open grassy slopes to the small cirque at the base of the North Face (about 7,360 ft). The North Face itself rises roughly 650 feet above the cirque, split by couloirs and a rock tower; the whole approach is considered short and easy relative to other Pasayten-area objectives.","approach_logistics":{"trailhead":"Tiffany Lake Trail","trailheadDirection":"Drive to Tiffany Springs Campground (elev. ~6,760 ft) via Forest Road 39, accessed either from Conconully (south, via FR-37) or from Winthrop (north, via East Chewuch Road and FR-37) - both are long gravel-road drives of an hour or more."},"approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"From the cirque, split the face in half: snow gullies left, rock tower and its ridge right. This route is on the right. A continuous snow chute above you means you are under the couloir line instead.

This route shares its start with the harder line on the same tower, and there is no way to separate them at the bottom, so do not try. Climb the rocky ridge from the cirque — roughly a hundred feet of fourth-class ground to gain the arete — and then take low-angled ridge travel along the crest with real exposure on both sides.

The split is at the vertical step, and it is the only test that works. Where the ridge steepens into a vertical section, this route bypasses it on the left and stays at fourth class. The other line goes straight up the tower into a wide flaring chimney and offwidth at 5.7 to 5.8. So: if you are looking at a chimney and reaching for wide gear, you have taken the harder line by accident. If you are moving left onto easier ground and never pull a hard move, you are on this route as intended.

Confirm by difficulty, which is unusual but honest here: five pitches, all of them fourth class or third, no technical crux anywhere. A pitch that feels like real rock climbing is evidence you are somewhere else. The route finishes with a short approach to the top of the tower and then a crest traverse of walking to Tiffany's main summit slope.

Negative marker on the descent: it is not reversed. From the top, descend the north-west ridge on mostly third-class ground to roughly 7,950 ft, contour north-east and find the old ridge trail — it may be faint — and follow it down to rejoin the main trail at Honeymoon Pass.","hazards":["Indistinguishable from the harder tower route until the vertical step, which is three pitches up","Loose rock and boulders throughout; the arete is exposed on both sides","The old descent trail is faint and easy to lose above the lower lake","No technical crux means parties move unroped where a slip is consequential","Long gravel drives from every direction"],"name":"Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass, then the east slope traverse","notes":"Drive to Tiffany Springs Campground at about 6,760 ft on the forest road system, reached either from Conconully to the south or from Winthrop to the north by the East Chewuch road. Both are long gravel drives of an hour or more; a third, gentler line comes over Baldy Pass on the South Fork.

From the campground, walk trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft, roughly forty-five minutes of easy trail. Leave the trail there and traverse south across open grassy slopes into the small cirque at the base of the north face, about 7,360 ft.

The face rises around six hundred and fifty feet above the cirque and is split by couloirs and a rock tower. The whole approach is short and easy by the standards of this corner of the state, which is the point of coming here.","season":"June through early September, once snow has cleared the lower sections"}]}

The trail's original bridge over Thunder Creek near mile 6.6 washed out in fall 2017; parties now cross via a log felled roughly 1,000 ft downstream of the old bridge site (about 900 ft upstream of the Thunder/McAllister Creek confluence). At McAllister Camp, leave the maintained trail and pick up the unmaintained climbers' boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and around downed timber up the north ridge; a viewpoint near 4,600 ft gives the first look at Primus, Tricouni, and neighboring peaks. Continue through forest and heather to Borealis Lake (base camp), a flat bench below the Borealis Glacier. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and follow the west edge of the Borealis Glacier — which has retreated significantly and split into upper and lower tiers separated by slabs and cliffs — navigating crevasses to Lucky Pass, the Primus-Tricouni col. From Lucky Pass, climb a steep snow finger roughly 200 ft up Tricouni's southwest side, then transition to rock ramps and ledges (class 3-4 scrambling) up the west ridge to the bouldery 8,102 ft summit. It is unmistakable from the col and there is no second candidate, and it is the entry to the climb. Above the snow the ground becomes rock ramps and ledges, class 3 to 4, following the west ridge to a bouldery summit. If you have left the col heading east onto a broad class 2-3 ridge, you are climbing Primus instead. orig: {"approach":"Start at the Niederprum Trailhead (Trail #653, ~918 ft) at the end of Old Mine Road. Because the Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded with boulders for years, you now park at the gate, scramble over the boulder barricade, and cross the old wooden bridge on foot to rejoin the road to the actual trailhead about 1.25 miles farther on — this detour adds roughly 2.6 miles round trip and 400 ft of extra gain beyond what older published mileages state. From the signed trailhead, Trail #653 switchbacks up through forest for about 1.3 miles, crossing into Boulder River Wilderness (marked by a small boundary sign) and passing an old slide-alder opening with views north to Darrington and the Sauk Valley. At roughly 3,200 ft you reach 'the flat,' a level clearing that was the site of Chas Niederprum's old mining cabin — a natural rest/camp spot with good views of the peak. Beyond the flat the maintained tread ends; continue on a climbers' boot path through thinning, brushy forest (deadfall to weave around) up to continuous snow around 2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. From there make a gently rising traverse south for about 0.5 mile into a wide, usually snow-filled couloir (holds snow into early July in normal years); ascend it to Lone Tree Pass (~4,970–5,000 ft, roughly 2 miles and 4,000+ ft above the trailhead — despite the name there are three trees near the pass, not one). From the pass, do a pleasant ridge traverse east for 600–700 m, then drop about 500 ft southeast through trees to a bench near a small lake/flat meadow at ~4,915 ft (a sheltered, view-blessed bivy option). Continue a long rising traverse east for roughly 2 km through forest and open slopes below cliff bands, then climb a gully/open slope to High Pass (~6,032–6,100 ft). Cross High Pass onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier and continue up snow (up to ~35° at the steepest) toward the summit snow ridge; rope up for crevasse hazard, which becomes real from roughly July onward. Key hazards along the way: the barricaded creek/bridge crossing at the start, avalanche-prone terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass, vague/brushy route-finding beyond 'the flat,' crevasses on the upper glacier in mid-to-late season, and the summit bergschrund/moat, which by midsummer often forces a short section of 5th-class rock or a delicate roped snow-bridge crossing just below the top. Parties stay on snow higher on the shoulder and face instead of threading the rock bands that appear later, keep climber's right on the glacier to avoid the worst crevassing, and meet a steep, sometimes icy rollover of about 50-55 degrees, the crux in these conditions. It is a popular ski and splitboard objective: many skin or boot the glacier basin and switch to crampons only for the final steep pitch below the summit, then ski back toward High Pass and Lone Tree Pass. {"approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"Same col, different first move — and you should know which you are doing before you leave the col. From the col southwest of the tower, this line goes straight up the sharp ridge above the col for about 100 ft. That ridge crest is the route. The south face line uses the same ground and then commits to the traverse right; both converge at the same Class 4 step and 5.5 move.

So the arrival test is the col, and it has three parts:
  1. You reached it by ascending snow or class 2 rock from the basin — not by crossing a steep snowfield, which is the west-side approach, and not by traversing across light rock under Dragontail's south ridge, which is the east face.
  2. Above you the ground rises as a defined, narrow crest rather than as an open face.
  3. The tower's summit block is directly above that crest, with the four-foot summit slot the last obstacle.

If the crest feels wrong: the ridge is sharp and exposed, and the recorded warning about this line is that placements on the crux are tricky to find. That is a route-finding statement as much as a protection one — a leader who cannot find gear may be a few feet off the correct line, on ground with fewer features.

And the common mistake: parties heading for the tower from Aasgard Pass drift too far east, toward Dragontail. The Hitchhiker begins roughly 100 ft further along the same traverse.","approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"From the South Arete base, head down and right along the base of the wall for about ten minutes to a start at double cracks beside a fir tree. A tree at the foot of a pair of cracks is the marker, and a tree is something you can walk into in cloud.

So the two checks are a duration and a tree: ten minutes of scrambling and traversing from the South Arete, and a fir. Not thirty seconds and not half an hour.

The negative test against its neighbour, and it is short and countable: the Hitchhiker begins roughly 100 ft further along the same traverse, at a small left-facing dihedral with four bolts. If you are standing at a dihedral with four bolts in it, you have gone 100 ft too far.

And if you have not lost height, you have not arrived: the traverse eventually drops away to skirt steeper terrain. Contouring level along the wall keeps you on South Arete ground.

Where it ends: the route is not commonly rappelled top to bottom. Parties top out and use the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete, third and fourth class with one short more exposed step, to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base, and out via the climber's trail to the Blue Lake Trail.","hazards":["Two routes starting about 100 ft apart on the same traverse","Loss of height along the base to skirt steeper terrain, which has to be regained","5.11d over seven pitches with no route-specific rappel line","No water on the approach"],"name":"Blue Lake Trail to the South Arete base, then down and right about ten minutes to the fir tree and double cracks","notes":"From the Blue Lake Trailhead, the climber's trail reaches the South Arete base in about an hour. Seven pitches at 5.11d, first climbed in October 1991.

The traverse to the start eventually drops away to skirt steeper terrain, so expect to lose height rather than contour.","season":"Jul-Sep"}]}

orig: {"approach":"Trailhead is the West Fork Buttermilk Creek Trailhead (Trail #411), reached via Twisp River Road ~10.7-10.8 miles from Twisp, then left on Buttermilk Creek Road, staying left onto East Buttermilk Road (Forest Road 43) for roughly 4 miles, then right onto the Road 500 spur for about 2.7 miles to the road-end trailhead at about 3,960 ft. From there Trail #411 climbs the West Fork Buttermilk Creek drainage into the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. Tread is inconsistently maintained in the lower-to-mid section — parties describe long stretches of blowdown with only brief clear tread, so plan to navigate by map/GPS rather than blazes. Several fords of the West Fork are the main early-season hazard: in June/early summer with high runoff these crossings can be genuinely difficult, sometimes requiring a detour upstream to find a log crossing. About 2 miles before Star Lake the trail enters the lowest larches, and roughly a half mile before the lake it crests Fish Creek Pass, an open viewpoint over the larch-covered Sawtooth Range and a good landmark/rest stop with reliable water nearby. From the pass, the trail drops slightly into the Star Lake basin (~7,460 ft) — 7.5 miles and about 3,500 ft of gain from the trailhead. Snow commonly lingers on the upper approach slopes into summer (encountered from roughly 6,000 ft up in early-season conditions), so a light axe/spikes are worth carrying outside of late-season. From Pete Lake, continue up the Lemah Creek/Lemah Meadows drainage (watch for windfall and thick vine maple in the meadow bypass) to join the Pacific Crest Trail; turn right (north) and climb the PCT's long switchback section roughly 4-4.5 more miles to Lower and Upper Vista Lake (~5,500-5,600 ft) — camp is commonly made here, making this a two-day approach of about 10 miles and 2,800 ft to reach the alpine basin. From there, traverse steep hardpan and talus (rockfall potential from parties above) up to a notch near 7,200 ft, then work into the southwest gully system — loose rock and an exposed, slightly outward-dipping slab lead through the final Class 2-3 scrambling to the summit. {"approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"The wall is clean white granite and it is visibly paler than what surrounds it, which is the first check that you are under the right formation. Follow the creek to the meadows and then up to the foot of it.

This route is the right-hand line. Start on the right side of the south face, on flakes, corners and splitters. Its neighbour begins with a layback off a large clean flake into a long left-facing corner system; if that is what is above you, walk right.

The defining feature is a broad ledge at half height, and it is the strongest thing this route has. Roughly halfway up the face the climbing arrives at a wide ledge that runs across the wall. That ledge is the route's hinge: from it you walk leftward before starting the upper half. A route that reaches a broad crossing ledge and then requires you to walk left along it is this one.

Confirm on the upper face. The first pitch above the ledge heads for the left side of the most prominent arete or pillar in the middle of the upper wall. That arete is the biggest feature up there and being on its left is the check. Two more pitches, then the line trends rightward to the summit.

The summit pitch separates the two routes absolutely. This one finishes on blocky ground just right of a prominent chimney. It does not go into the chimney. The neighbouring route tops out through a deep summit chimney. So: blocky ground beside a slot means this route; stemming up inside the slot means you have crossed onto the other line.

Negative marker lower down, since the two lines are close: if there was no broad crossing ledge and instead you moved rightward under a roof into a splitter to reach a smaller ledge, you are on the neighbour.

Descent is not separately documented for this line. Because it shares the summit and the mid-face ledge with its neighbour, parties use that route's rappels down the south-east side: a seventy-metre rope, sparse fixed anchors, and enough webbing to build your own. Treat that as an inference rather than a described descent and go up prepared to make anchors.","hazards":["The Wine Spires pullout and its climbers' trail lead to the far side of the crest, not to this face","Its own descent is not separately documented; the shared rappel line is an inference from the shared summit","Rappel anchors are sparse and some must be built; carry extra webbing","Rarely climbed, so there is no chalk, no traffic and no current conditions information","Two long routes on one face that share a mid-height ledge and a summit"],"name":"Cedar Creek trail from the highway, then the creek draining the south side","notes":"The Spires Trail is the wrong approach for this face. The unsigned pullout further west and the col above it serve the spires on the other side of the crest, not the southern wall this route is on.

Take the Cedar Creek trail from its own trailhead off the highway. At roughly five miles, turn off to the right below the old burn; a rough path then follows the right-hand side of the creek draining the south side of the formation. Meadows at about 6,200 ft give good camping.

This is a quiet corner by the standards of this highway. There is no established climbers' camp, no fixed approach gear and effectively no traffic.

A parking pass or day fee covers the trailhead; there is no permit system and no quota on national forest ground here.","season":"Roughly mid-June through late September; July and August are typically driest"}],"descent_text":"No descent is separately documented for The Chalice. Because The Chalice shares its summit and a mid-face crossing ledge with Playing Not Spraying, the same SE-side rappel line is very likely used for both — this is an inference from the shared-summit/shared-ledge relationship, not a confirmed fact for The Chalice itself. Playing Not Spraying's first-ascent party rappelled the SE side of the peak on a single 70m rope, noting only natural anchors (trees, horns) and advising extra bulk webbing."}

orig: {"approach":"Access starts on Ross Lake: from the Ross Dam trailhead on SR-20 (near milepost 134), hike the short Ross Dam Trail down to Ross Lake Resort, then take the resort's water taxi (or paddle a canoe) roughly 20+ miles up-lake to the Little Beaver Creek dock at the lake's north end. From the dock, follow the maintained (but lightly traveled) Little Beaver Trail west, paralleling Little Beaver Creek through cedar-fir forest with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, about 4.6-5 miles to Perry Creek Camp/Shelter, a three-sided log shelter that marks the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward the Mox massif. From Perry Creek Camp there is no trail: the standard line follows the Perry Creek drainage south, and staying in or right beside the creekbed itself gives the fastest travel (easy rock-hopping and scrambling) up to about 3,600 ft, where dense slide alder chokes the creek and forces climbers up onto a bank. The south (true left) side of the drainage is preferred here — it holds older, more open forest and fewer avalanche paths, while the north side is a nearly impenetrable slide-alder thicket.
